results.finding: Rare cases of concurrent acute inflammatory polyradiculoneuropathy and primary NMJ autoimmunity have been documented; post-infectious immune dysregulation can trigger new-onset NMJ disease; IVIG given for one autoimmune neurologic disorder may paradoxically trigger or accelerate another; anti-GQ1b antibodies, characteristic of Miller Fisher-variant polyradiculoneuropathy, are not features of postsynaptic NMJ disease.

results.finding: Post-infectious immune activation can trigger multiple simultaneous autoimmune neurological conditions; GBS and MG can coexist as distinct diagnoses with separate pathophysiology

output.summary: Concurrent GBS and MG is rare but documented. Key distinction: GBS causes ascending paralysis with areflexia (post-synaptic peripheral demyelination); MG causes fatigable weakness with NMJ dysfunction. Cranial nerve involvement in the setting of GBS should prompt evaluation for concurrent MG, especially when fatigable pattern is present.

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup

avoided_actions.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Brain MRI is non-contributory in typical MG; reserve for cases where an alternative CNS cause (brainstem lesion, demyelination) is genuinely in the differential.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

accepted: Myasthenia gravis, AChR antibody-positive, generalized (MGFA Class IIb), new onset after recent Guillain-Barré syndrome (sequential/concurrent autoimmunity)

differential.key_features: GBS recurrence/relapse is possible but typically presents with ascending weakness and areflexia, not fatigable ocular/bulbar weakness; AChR positive here.
CIDP would show demyelination on NCS; here NCS does not match.
MFS gives ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia; anti-GQ1b negative; reflexes preserved; pattern fluctuating not monophasic.
No focal MRI findings; fluctuating pattern not vascular.
Objective RNS decrement and AChR positivity rule out functional etiology.

key_clinical_evidence: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
GBS and MG are both antibody-mediated; sequential/overlapping autoimmunity is uncommon but documented and should not lead to anchoring on the first diagnosis.
Diffuse thymic enlargement (not a discrete mass) is common in AChR+ MG and typically reflects thymic hyperplasia — thymectomy may still be considered.

patient.history_present_illness: A 42-year-old man was re-admitted to neurology after developing new bilateral ptosis and diplopia 4 weeks after discharge from a prior hospitalization for acute ascending weakness attributed to Guillain-Barré syndrome. During the prior admission, he had presented with ascending leg weakness over 5 days, areflexia, and mild sensory symptoms. Nerve conduction studies reportedly showed mild demyelinating features and he received a 5-day course of IVIG with partial improvement in leg strength. He was discharged with mild residual leg weakness and sensory symptoms on gabapentin. However, over the 2 weeks following discharge, he developed new bilateral eyelid drooping and double vision — which had NOT been present during his initial GBS presentation or hospitalization. He initially thought this was a GBS progression, but his prior GBS presentation had no cranial nerve involvement. The new symptoms have a clear diurnal variation: worse at the end of the day, significantly better after sleep. He also reports jaw fatigue during meals. His girlfriend has noticed his voice becomes nasal after prolonged conversations. He denies any respiratory symptoms, dysphagia, or return of the ascending leg weakness. He is otherwise improving from his GBS symptoms. The combination of incomplete GBS recovery with new cranial NMJ-pattern symptoms prompted readmission for clarification.

neurological_exam.additional: NIF -46 cmH2O (borderline). No dysphagia currently. Clinical picture confusing: partial GBS recovery plus new NMJ findings.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: New bilateral ptosis over past 2 weeks — left greater than right. Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze (left complete at 40 seconds). New horizontal diplopia on rightward gaze. Pupils equal, reactive. Mild facial weakness bilaterally. Dysarthria after 3 minutes sustained speech.
neurological_exam.motor: Proximal upper extremity 4/5. Proximal lower extremity 4/5. Distal 5/5. Fatigable weakness on exam. DTRs 1+ throughout (prior GBS partially recovered).
neurological_exam.reflexes: Hyporeflexia 1+ throughout (residual from GBS). Plantar downgoing.
neurological_exam.sensory: Mild stocking decrease to light touch bilaterally (residual GBS sensory involvement).
